background:
Philemon: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

Study notes · dates are approximate and scholars vary

At a glance

Philemon is Paul's shortest letter, a personal appeal to a wealthy believer in Colossae on behalf of his slave Onesimus, who had run away, met Paul in prison and become a Christian. Paul sends him back, around AD 60–62, “no longer as a servant, but… a brother beloved” (v. 16).

QuestionTraditional viewNotes
AuthorPaul, with Timothy (v. 1)Accepted by virtually all scholars as Paul's.
Date and placeAbout AD 60–62, from prison, probably in RomeSent at the same time as Colossians, carried by Tychicus with Onesimus (Col 4:7–9).
RecipientsPhilemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church in Philemon's house (v. 1–2)Apphia may be Philemon's wife and Archippus his son. Though personal, the letter was read to the whole church.
OnesimusA slave of Philemon who had wronged him (v. 18)His name means “useful.” Paul plays on it: once “unprofitable,” now “profitable” (v. 11).
Length25 verses, about 335 words in GreekAbout the length of a typical private letter of the time.
What happened next?UnknownAround AD 110 Ignatius wrote to a bishop of Ephesus named Onesimus; some think he was the same man.

Without commanding, Paul appeals to love and to the new relationship master and slave now share in Christ.

The time map

The shaded band marks AD 60–62, Paul's house arrest in Rome, when Onesimus came to him.

Slavery in the Roman world

Philemon cannot be understood without Roman slavery, which touched nearly every household and church.

  • How common. Perhaps a third of Italy's people and a large share in eastern cities were slaves. They worked as farmhands, craftsmen, teachers, doctors and household managers.
  • Legal status. A slave was legally property. Masters could punish, sell or free them, though some cruelty was frowned on.
  • Runaways. Runaway slaves (fugitivi) could be hunted down, beaten, branded or chained. Harboring one was a legal risk.
  • Seeking an advocate. A slave in trouble might flee to a friend of the master to plead for him. The Roman writer Pliny the Younger wrote such a letter to a friend, about a freedman, around AD 100; Paul's letter is similar but goes much further.
  • Freedom. Many slaves were freed in time and became citizens or clients of their former owners. Paul hints at more than forgiveness: “thou wilt do even beyond what I say” (v. 21).
  • Brothers in Christ. In the church, slave and master shared the same table, the same Lord and the same family name, “brother” (Col 3:11; Gal 3:28).

Paul does not attack slavery as a legal system in this letter, but he plants a principle that would eventually undermine it: the slave is “a brother beloved… both in the flesh and in the Lord.”

Colossae and Philemon's household

Philemon was a well-off believer in Colossae, a small city in the Lycus valley of western Asia Minor (Türkiye).

  • A house church. The church met in Philemon's home, large enough to host a group of believers (v. 2).
  • Converted through Paul. Philemon owed his own spiritual life to Paul (v. 19), probably meeting him in Ephesus.
  • Onesimus' journey. Onesimus somehow reached Paul in prison, about 1,200 miles away in Rome if Paul was there, or about 120 miles in Ephesus if Paul was imprisoned there.
  • The return. Onesimus traveled home with Tychicus, who carried Colossians and probably Ephesians too (Col 4:7–9).
  • Paul's request. “Prepare me also a lodging” (v. 22): Paul hoped to be released and to visit Colossae.
  • Laodicea nearby. Ten miles away; the letters were to be shared between the churches (Col 4:16).

Around the world in AD 60–62

Philemon was written as Nero's good years were ending.

RegionWhat was happening
BritainBoudica's revolt (AD 60–61). The queen of the Iceni burned London, Colchester and St Albans before being crushed.
RomeNero's early good years ended about AD 62. The Great Fire of AD 64 was followed by the first persecution of Christians.
JudeaTension grew; James the Lord's brother was killed in AD 62. The Jewish revolt broke out in AD 66.
Armenia and ParthiaA compromise peace in AD 63; Nero crowned the Parthian prince Tiridates king of Armenia in Rome in AD 66.
ItalyAn earthquake damaged Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 62, seventeen years before Vesuvius buried them.
ChinaThe Eastern Han dynasty under Emperor Ming; silk reached Rome along the trade routes.
IndiaThe Kushan Empire was forming in the northwest; tradition says Thomas preached in India.
The AmericasTeotihuacan was growing; the Moche and Nazca cultures flourished in Peru.

Maps: then and now

Colossae lay in the Lycus valley, on the main road east from Ephesus. Onesimus may have traveled that road to reach Paul.

Today Colossae is an unexcavated mound near Honaz, Türkiye, though survey work has begun. Nearby Laodicea and Hierapolis have been extensively excavated.

How the setting shapes the study

Every line of Philemon has a background in Roman household life.

PassageConnection to the times
Phlm 1–2Wealthy believers hosted churches in their homes.
Phlm 8–9Paul could command but chooses to appeal “for love's sake.”
Phlm 10“My child, whom I have begotten in my bonds”: Onesimus was converted in prison.
Phlm 11Onesimus means “useful”; Paul plays on the name.
Phlm 15–16“No longer as a servant, but more than a servant, a brother beloved.”
Phlm 18–19Paul writes an IOU in his own hand, like a legal promissory note.
Phlm 21“Beyond what I say” may hint at freeing Onesimus.
Phlm 22Guests depended on hospitality; Paul hopes to visit.
Phlm 23–24The same companions appear in Colossians 4, tying the letters together.

Paul offers to take Onesimus' debt on himself, a picture of what Christ has done for us.

items.text: Greeting vv. 1–3
Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon our beloved and fellow-worker,
and to Apphia our sister, and to Archippus our fellow-soldier, and to the church in thy house:
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Philemon's Love and Faith vv. 4–7
I thank my God always, making mention of thee in my prayers,
hearing of thy love, and of the faith which thou hast toward the Lord Jesus, and toward all the saints;
that the fellowship of thy faith may become effectual, in the knowledge of every good thing which is in you, unto Christ.
For I had much joy and comfort in thy love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through thee, brother.
Paul's Plea for Onesimus vv. 8–16
Wherefore, though I have all boldness in Christ to enjoin thee that which is befitting,
yet for love’s sake I rather beseech, being such a one as Paul the aged, and now a prisoner also of Christ Jesus:
I beseech thee for my child, whom I have begotten in my bonds, Onesimus,
who once was unprofitable to thee, but now is profitable to thee and to me:
whom I have sent back to thee in his own person, that is, my very heart:
whom I would fain have kept with me, that in thy behalf he might minister unto me in the bonds of the gospel:
but without thy mind I would do nothing; that thy goodness should not be as of necessity, but of free will.
For perhaps he was therefore parted from thee for a season, that thou shouldest have him for ever;
no longer as a servant, but more than a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much rather to thee, both in the flesh and in the Lord.
Paul's Promise vv. 17–22
If then thou countest me a partner, receive him as myself.
But if he hath wronged thee at all, or oweth thee aught, put that to mine account;
I Paul write it with mine own hand, I will repay it: that I say not unto thee that thou owest to me even thine own self besides.
Yea, brother, let me have joy of thee in the Lord: refresh my heart in Christ.
Having confidence in thine obedience I write unto thee, knowing that thou wilt do even beyond what I say.
But withal prepare me also a lodging: for I hope that through your prayers I shall be granted unto you.
Final Greetings vv. 23–25
Epaphras, my fellow-prisoner in Christ Jesus, saluteth thee;
and so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, my fellow-workers.
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

questions.label: OBSERVE
questions.text: How does Paul describe Onesimus in verses 10–16, and what does he ask Philemon to do with him?

questions.label: THEN
questions.text: In a Roman world where a runaway slave could be severely punished, how bold was Paul's request to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother (v. 16)?

questions.label: NOW
questions.text: Paul offers to pay whatever Onesimus owes (vv. 18–19); where might you be called to stand between others and help bring reconciliation?

wrap.title: Philemon In Summary
paras: Philemon is a short, personal letter, but it carries a powerful message. Onesimus, a slave belonging to Philemon of Colossae, had run away, perhaps after stealing from his master. Somehow he met Paul in prison and became a believer. Now Paul sends him back with this letter, asking Philemon to receive him not as a slave but as a beloved brother.

Paul writes with great tact. He begins by praising Philemon's love and faith, and the way he refreshes the hearts of the saints. Though he could command, he appeals instead for love's sake, as “Paul the aged, and now a prisoner also of Christ Jesus.” He calls Onesimus “my child, whom I have begotten in my bonds,” and says that sending him back is like sending his own heart.

Paul sees God's hand in what happened: perhaps Onesimus was separated from Philemon for a while so that he could have him back forever, “no longer as a servant, but more than a servant, a brother beloved.” In Christ, the relationship between master and slave has been transformed.

Paul then offers to pay whatever Onesimus owes, writing an IOU in his own hand: “put that to mine account.” This is a beautiful picture of the gospel, in which Christ takes our debt on Himself. Paul adds that he is confident Philemon will do even more than he asks, perhaps hinting at freedom, and asks him to prepare a guest room.

The message in one line: the gospel makes former enemies into brothers, calls believers to forgive and receive one another as Christ has received them, and changes even the hardest relationships of this world.
